A massive landslide has partially blocked the Chameliya River in Darchula district, prompting authorities to evacuate local families and issue a high alert for downstream communities . The incident occurred in the Bhattar area of Api Himal Rural Municipality-1, just days after a devastating flood killed over 1,200 people in the region .

THE LANDSLIDE AND IMMEDIATE RESPONSE

The landslide sent a huge volume of debris into the Chameliya River on Friday, completely blocking its flow for approximately half an hour . While the river has since managed to carve a path through the debris, officials warn that further slides could cause a complete blockage . The unstable slope remains active, with continuous rockfall reported .

The District Administration Office has urged residents along the riverbanks to remain "vigilant" and be prepared for sudden flooding, as a blockage can create a temporary reservoir that may burst catastrophically . At least 15 families have been relocated from the high-risk Bhattar settlement to safer areas . Police and Armed Police Force personnel have been mobilized to monitor the situation . Authorities have released emergency contact numbers for residents to report any changes .

A REGIONAL THREAT AND A SECONDARY CRISIS

The risk is not confined to Nepal. Officials have warned that a sudden release of water could impact areas along the Chameliya River corridor and its confluence with the Kali River, potentially affecting communities in both Nepal and India . The region is already reeling from a catastrophic flash flood on August 26, which was caused by a glacier collapse . The death toll from that disaster has now reached 1,287, with over 5,000 people still missing .

A BUZZ AIRLINE TALE. LIFE ON THE LINE.

The wheels of the Delta 737-900 settled on the runway with a soft chirp after six long hours across America,  a redeye from Seattle to Miami-nothing but black sky, brilliant stars, an occasional thunderstorm firing off in the distance, glowing instruments, and a cockpit full of quiet exhaustion. 

I taxied in weary of the flight and ever-mindful that a taxi accident was a career ender. First, we spool down the first engine to save fuel…with that familiar whine that always sounded like a sigh of relief.

After navigating a sometimes strange airport to the crew van pickup spot, the  van dropped me and  my  crew at the hotel just before dawn. 

The Hyatt Regency in downtown Miami, one of those towering glass-and-steel beasts that looks like it could launch rockets. 

I pushed through the revolving doors with my crew, flight bag in one hand and my crew roller board dragging from my other, uniform rumpled but still crisp enough to command respect. Tie pulled tight. 

The lobby smelled of fresh coffee, faint lemon polish, and that universal hotel scent—clean sheets and quiet ambition. A few early birds shuffled around with their roller bags, eyes puffy like mine.

“We’re Delta 1090,” I told the smiling front-desk gal, sliding my ID across the marble counter. She slid a clipboard of crew names and we all signed in.

She typed fast, her fingers clicking like rain on the windshield at 35,000 feet. “Welcome back, sir. Long night?”

I followed at a distance, belly low, because that is what a dog does when the world changes size.
